questions.html:
Match the following :

$\begin{array}{clcl}  \text{(1)} & \text{Determinants}  & \text{(a)}\ & \text{No attribute can be added} \\   \text{(2)} & \text{Candidate key}  & \text{(b)}\ & \text{Uniquely identified a row} \\  \text{(3)} & \text{Non-redundancy}  & \text{(c)}\ & \text{A constraint between two attribute} \\   \text{(4)} & \text{Functional Dependency}  & \text{(d)}\ & \text{Group of attributes on the left hand} \\ &&&  \text{side of arrow of function dependency.} \\  \end{array}$
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 4)

The correct matching is:

1-d, 2-b, 3-a, 4-c

Determinants: (d) Group of attributes on the left-hand side of the arrow of functional dependency.

Candidate key: (b) Uniquely identifies a row.

Non-redundancy: (a) No attribute can be added.

Functional Dependency: (c) A constraint between two attributes.

Option A is the answer

Which of the following statements is true?

$D_1$: The decomposition of the schema R(A, B, C) into R$_1$(A,B) and R$_2$(A,C) is always lossless

$D_2$: The decomposition of the schema R(A, B, C, D, E) having AD $\rightarrow$ B, C $\rightarrow$ DE, B $\rightarrow$ AE, and AE $\rightarrow$ C, into R$_1$(A,B, D) and R$_2$(A, C, D, E) is lossless
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Selected solution (score: 11)

Ans. D

D1: Counter ex. for D1. Assume B->A and C->A. Now in R1, R2  A is common attribute but it is not a superkey in any of decomposed relation. Hence this decomposition is NOT ALWAYS lossless.

 

D2: As (AD) is a common attribute between R1, R2 and (AD) -> R1 ie AD is superkey in relation R1.Hence, it is lossless Decomposition.

Therefore, only D2 is True.

Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 3)

Super Key: A super key is a set of one or more attributes(columns) that can uniquely identify a tuple(row) in a relation(table).
Candidate Key: A candidate key is a minimal super key, meaning it has no redundant attributes. Every candidate key is a super key, but not all super keys are candidate keys.
Primary Key: A primary key is one of the candidate keys chosen by the database designer to uniquely identify tuples in the relation.

Thus, the relationship is: 
- Every primary key is a candidate key.
- Every candidate key is a super key.

Thus option B is the answer.

primary key ⊆ candidate key ⊆ super key

questions.html:
In relational database management, which of the following is/are property/properties of candidate key?

P: Uniqueness

Q: Irreducibility
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 6)

Uniqueness: A candidate key must uniquely identify each tuple(row) in the relation(table).

Irreducibility: A candidate key must be minimal, meaning no proper subset of the candidate key can uniquely identify each row.

Option C is correct 

Both P and Q

questions.html: Suppose R is a relation schema and F is a set of functional dependencies on R. Further, suppose R1 and R2 form a decomposition of R. Then the decomposition is a lossless join decomposition of R provided that:

options.html: both R1∩R2→R1 and R1∩R2→R2 functional dependencies are in F+
at least one from R1∩R2→R1 and R1∩R2→R2 is in F+

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 7)

A decomposition of a relation schema \( R \) into \( R_1 \) and \( R_2 \) is a lossless join decomposition if at least one of the following functional dependencies is in \( F^+ \) (the closure of \( F \)):

- \( R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_1 \)
- \( R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_2 \)

This ensures that when \( R_1 \) and \( R_2 \) are joined back together, no spurious tuples are introduced, and the original relation \( R \) can be accurately reconstructed.

Thus, option D is correct

at least one from \( R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_1 \) and \( R_1 \cap R_2 \rightarrow R_2 \) is in \( F^+ \)

options.html: A relation in BCNF is always in 3NF
A relation in 3NF is always in BCNF
A relation in BCNF is not in 3NF

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Selected solution (score: 1)

  • The correct answer is A. A relation in BCNF is always in 3NF.

  • 3NF: A table is in 3NF if it follows these rules:

    • It is already in 2NF (which eliminates partial dependencies).
    • There are no transitive dependencies for non-prime attributes (a non-prime attribute is any attribute that is not part of the candidate key). In simpler terms, all non-key attributes must be solely dependent on the entire candidate key, and not on any part of it.

  • BCNF: A table is in BCNF if it adheres to all the rules of 3NF, and additionally:

    • Every determinant (an attribute or set of attributes that determines another attribute) in the table must be a candidate key.

Because BCNF has stricter requirements, a table that satisfies BCNF will inherently also satisfy all the requirements of 3NF.

The other answer choices are incorrect because:

  • B. A relation in 3NF is always in BCNF: This is not always true. A table can be in 3NF but violate the determinant rule of BCNF.
  • C. BCNF and 3NF are same: As explained earlier, BCNF is a stricter form of 3NF.
  • D. A relation in BCNF is not in 3NF: This contradicts the core principle of BCNF adhering to all the rules of 3NF.

questions.html:
Armstrong $(1974)$ proposed systematic approach to derive functional dependencies. Match the following w.r.t functional dependencies:

$$\begin{array}{}  & \textbf{List-I}  && \textbf{List -II} \\  \text{a.} &  \text{Decomposition Rule} & \text{i.} & \text{If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $Z \rightarrow W$ then $\{X,Z\} \rightarrow \{Y, W\}$} \\  \text{b.} &  \text{Union rule} & \text{ii.} & \text{If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $\{Y, W\} \rightarrow Z$ then $\{X, W\} \rightarrow Z$} \\  \text{c.} &  \text{Composition rule} & \text{iii.} & \text{If $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$ then $X \rightarrow \{Y, Z\}$} \\  \text{d.} &  \text{Psedudo transitivity rule} & \text{iv.} & \text{ If $X \rightarrow \{Y, Z\}$ then $X \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow Z$} \\  \end{array}$$

Codes:
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 4)

Answer is option $\boxed{D}$

These all are Armostrong Inference Rules:

  1. Decomposition Rule: If $X \to YZ$ then $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$
  2. Union Rule : If $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$ then $X \to YZ$
  3. Composition Rule: If $X \to Y$ and $A \to B$ then $XA \to YB$
  4. PesudoTransitivity Rule: If $X \to Y$ and $YZ \to W$ then $XZ \to W$

reference wikipedia

questions.html:
Consider a relational schema $S=(U,V,W,X,Y,Z)$ on which the following functional dependencies hold:

$(U \rightarrow V, VW \rightarrow X, Y \rightarrow W, X \rightarrow U)$

Which are the candidate keys among following options?
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 2)

A Candidate Key is the minimal set of attributes that can functionally determine all attributes of the relation.

Given the functional dependencies:

\(U \to V\)

\(VW \to X\)

\(Y \to W\)

\(X \to U\)

The attributes that are not on the RHS of any FD are:

\(Y\), \(Z\)

So, \(Y\) and \(Z\) must be part of any candidate key as no other attribute or set of attributes can derive them.

Next, let's determine the minimal sets of attributes that can determine all other attributes by including \(Y\) and \(Z\) and checking the closures of these sets:

\(YZ^+\):

\(YZ^+ = \{Y, Z, W\}\)

Thus, \(YZ\) is not sufficient to determine all attributes of \(S\).

Now, let's check combinations of other attributes with \(YZ\).

First, single attribute combinations:

\(UYZ^+\):

\(UYZ^+ = \{U, V, W, X, Y, Z\}\)

Thus, \(UYZ\) determines all attributes \(\{U, V, W, X, Y, Z\}\).

\(VYZ^+\):

\(VYZ^+ = \{V, U, W, X, Y, Z\}\)

Thus, \(VYZ\) determines all attributes \(\{V, U, W, X, Y, Z\}\).

\(XYZ^+\):

\(XYZ^+ = \{X, U, V, W, Y, Z\}\)

Thus, \(XYZ\) determines all attributes \(\{X, U, V, W, Y, Z\}\).

So, the candidate keys are:

\(UYZ\), \(VYZ\), \(XYZ\)

Therefore, option D is correct answer

\(UYZ\), \(VYZ\), \(XYZ\)

questions.html: The best normal form of relation scheme $R(A, B, C, D)$ along with the set of functional dependencies $F = \left\{AB \rightarrow C, AB \rightarrow D, C \rightarrow A, D \rightarrow B\right\}$ is
questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 7)

Given relation \( R(A, B, C, D) \) with the functional dependencies \( F = \{ AB \rightarrow C, AB \rightarrow D, C \rightarrow A, D \rightarrow B \} \). 

Determining the Candidate Keys

\( AB \), \(AD\), \(BC\) and \( CD \) are the candidate keys, as they both determine all attributes in the relation.

1. First Normal Form (1NF)

The relation is in 1NF since it contains only atomic values.

2. Second Normal Form (2NF)

A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key.

  • All attributes \( A, B, C, D \) are part of the candidate keys, making them prime attributes.
  • Since there are no non-prime attributes, the relation is trivially in 2NF.

3. Third Normal Form (3NF)

A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and no transitive dependencies exist, meaning no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key.

  • All attributes \( A, B, C, D \) are prime attributes.
  • Since there are no non-prime attributes, the relation is trivially in 3NF.

4. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)

A relation is in BCNF if for every functional dependency \( X \rightarrow Y \), \( X \) is a superkey.

  • Functional dependencies \( C \rightarrow A \) and \( D \rightarrow B \) do not have \( C \) and \( D \) as superkeys.
  • Therefore, the relation violates BCNF.

Conclusion

The relation \( R(A, B, C, D) \) with the given functional dependencies is in 3NF but not in BCNF because there are functional dependencies where the left-hand side is not a superkey.

So, the relation is in 3NF but not in BCNF. Therefore, Option B is correct.

questions.html:
Consider the following relational schemes for a library database:

Book (Title, Author, Catalog_no, Publisher, Year, Price)
Collection(Title, Author, Catalog_no)

with the following functional dependencies:

  1. $\text{Title Author }\rightarrow\text{ Catalog_no}$

  2. $\text{Catalog_no }\rightarrow\text{ Title Author Publisher Year}$

  3. $\text{Publisher Title Year}\rightarrow\text{ Price}$

Assume $\left\{\text{ Author, Title }\right\}$ is the key for both schemes. Which of the following statements is $\text{true}$?

options.html: Both Book and Collection are in $\text{3NF}$ only
Both Book and Collection are in $\text{2NF}$ only

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Selected solution (score: 7)

Detailed Video Solution, with Complete & Correct Analysis: https://youtu.be/ldl47NMWciE 

Source:

https://gateoverflow.in/492/gate-cse-2008-question-69

https://gateoverflow.in/56753/ugc-net-cse-june-2014-part-3-question-22

Watch Above Video Solution for Correct Understanding.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

My analysis:

Collection:

Candidate keys are {Title, Author} and {Catalog_no}, since:
- Title, Author -> Catalog_no
- Catalog_no -> Title, Author

Hence, every non-trivial FD has a superkey on the LHS. Therefore, Collection is in BCNF.

Book:

Candidate keys are {Title, Author} and {Catalog_no}.

The relation is in 2NF because no proper subset of the composite candidate key {Title, Author} determines any non-prime attribute.

However, the FD

Publisher, Title, Year -> Price

violates 3NF because:
- {Publisher, Title, Year} is not a superkey.
- Price is a non-prime attribute.

Also,

Catalog_no -> Publisher, Title, Year
Publisher, Title, Year -> Price

imply

Catalog_no -> Price.

Although this forms a dependency chain, the actual reason for the 3NF violation is the FD Publisher, Title, Year -> Price, where the LHS is not a superkey and the RHS is a non-prime attribute.

Therefore, Book is in 2NF but not in 3NF, while Collection is in BCNF. Hence, Option C is the correct answer.
